w1101-01-bomber-holes: These bombers came back shot full of holes, and survivorship bias almost sent the armor to the wrong place. In the famous World War Two story, most of the holes were on the wings, the tail and the body, so the obvious idea was more armor right there. But the statistician Abraham Wald asked where the missing holes were. Planes hit in the engines mostly never made it home, so nobody got to count those holes. They were only looking at the planes that survived. So you put the armor where the holes aren't.
w1101-02-guard-faint: This guard is about to show you why soldiers faint. He hasn't moved for a long time. See, the veins in your legs can't push blood back up to your heart on their own. Every time your calf muscles tighten, they squeeze those veins, and little valves keep the blood from sliding back down. So your calves work like a pump. But when you stand frozen, that pump mostly stops. Blood pools in his legs, less gets back to his heart, so less reaches his brain, and down he goes. That's why guards wiggle their toes and tense their calves. It keeps the pump going, and keeps them on their feet.
w1101-03-speed-camera: She braked for both speed cameras, and the mean value theorem still says she was speeding. These cameras don't care how fast you pass them. They time you between them. She covered ten miles in eight minutes. That's an average of seventy five miles an hour, and the limit's sixty five. Her position changed smoothly, with no jumps, so the theorem says at some moment she was going exactly seventy five. So the ticket's fair, even though she was slow at both cameras.
w1101-04-cane-toads: Australia brought in about a hundred cane toads to save its sugar cane, and it backfired badly. The beetles they were supposed to eat lived mostly up high on the cane, where the toads couldn't reach. So the toads ate almost everything else. And they're poisonous, so many animals that tried eating them died. Back home in the Americas, predators and diseases helped keep them in check. In Australia, almost nothing did, and that's how a newcomer becomes an invasive species. Now there are millions of them, all from that first shipment. Free practice for this on level prep dot com.
